aliases: Rasul Allah (the Messenger of God, in Islamic usage)

roles: religious and political leader of the community at Medina
prophet and messenger of God (in Islamic belief)
summary: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah (c. 570 to 632 CE) was an Arabian religious and political leader from Mecca and the founding figure of Islam, who from about 610 preached monotheism in Mecca, emigrated to Medina in 622 (the Hijra, year 1 of the hijri calendar), and died there in 11/632 as leader of a community extending over much of Arabia. Muslims hold him to be the Messenger of God and the last of the prophets, to whom the Qur'an was revealed.
description:
Muhammad is approached here in two clearly separated registers: the life as reconstructed by historical scholarship, given as scholarship, and the claims of the Islamic tradition about him, given as attributed confession. The editor neither affirms nor denies any confessional claim.

On the historical side, the standard narrative, drawn from the Muslim biographical tradition, which historians such as Watt and Donner treat as broadly usable, a judgment contested by the scholars discussed below, runs as follows. Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE into the clan of Hashim of the tribe of Quraysh; orphaned young, he was raised by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then his uncle Abu Talib, took part in the caravan trade, and married Khadija, a widow merchant. Around 610 (about twelve years before the Hijra) he began to proclaim messages that he presented as revelations from God, calling his hearers to worship one God and warning of a coming judgment. He gained a small following in Mecca and met growing opposition from leading men of Quraysh. After the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib, negotiations with men of Yathrib led to the emigration (Hijra) of his followers and then of Muhammad himself in 622, the year later fixed as year 1 of the hijri calendar; Yathrib became known as Medina. There he led a community whose arrangements with its neighbours are preserved in the document known as the Constitution of Medina, and waged a series of conflicts with Mecca (Badr, 2/624; Uhud, 3/625; the Trench, 5/627), concluded the truce of al-Hudaybiyya (6/628), and entered Mecca in 8/630. He died in Medina in 11/632, by which time much of Arabia had entered into alliance with him. Historians interpret this career differently: W. Montgomery Watt read him as prophet and statesman responding to the social and economic tensions of Meccan society, while Fred Donner stresses the religious, eschatological motivation of what he calls the early Believers movement.

The sources for this life are themselves the subject of a long scholarly debate, recorded here without adjudication. The Qur'an, which Muslims hold to be the revelation he received, is treated by most historians as the earliest source bearing on Muhammad, but it offers few narrative details. The detailed narrative comes from the sira and maghazi literature and the hadith, whose earliest surviving full biography is Ibn Ishaq's (d. c. 150/767) as transmitted in the recension of Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833), compiled well over a century after Muhammad's death. Revisionist scholarship questioned how far these later sources can be used to reconstruct events: John Wansbrough read the sira as a literary salvation history shaped by later interconfessional concerns, and Patricia Crone and Michael Cook, in Hagarism (1977), proposed an exploratory reconstruction from seventh-century non-Muslim sources that departs sharply from the Muslim account. Other scholars responded that parts of the tradition can be dated much earlier: Gregor Schoeler and Harald Motzki, using analysis of chains of transmission together with textual variants, trace some biographical reports to transmitters of the late first century AH such as Urwa ibn al-Zubayr (d. c. 94/713) and al-Zuhri (d. 124/742), and Donner argued for the early character of the Qur'anic text and its community. Motzki summarised the dilemma as the difficulty of writing a critical biography when the sources that make a biography possible are precisely those whose reliability is in question.

In Islamic belief, Muhammad is the Messenger of God (rasul Allah) and the seal of the prophets (khatam al-nabiyyin, Q 33:40), the last in a line of prophets that Muslims hold includes Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa. Muslims hold that the Qur'an was revealed to him by God through the angel Gabriel (Jibril) over about twenty-three years, beginning in the cave of Hira near Mecca with the words 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created' (Q 96:1), as narrated from Aisha in the opening book of Sahih al-Bukhari. The tradition insists on his full humanity: the Qur'an has him say 'I am only a man like you, to whom has been revealed that your god is one God' (Q 18:110), and Muslims do not regard him as divine or as an object of worship. In Islamic belief the Qur'an is his principal miracle (mu'jiza), while the hadith and sira report further miracles; the Night Journey and Ascension (al-isra wa-l-mi'raj) are linked by the tradition to Q 17:1. His words and practice (sunna), transmitted as hadith, are held by Muslims to be a source of law and guidance second only to the Qur'an, and Muslim devotion accords him an exemplary place. Sunni, Shi'i, and Ibadi Muslims share these convictions and differ over his succession: Shi'i tradition holds that he designated Ali as his successor, notably at Ghadir Khumm, while Sunni tradition accepts the leadership of Abu Bakr as the first caliph, and Ibadis, like Sunnis, accept Abu Bakr's caliphate. Tarif Khalidi traces how Muslim portrayals of him changed across the centuries, from the early sira and hadith to modern biographies; Jonathan A. C. Brown sets out the Muslim account alongside the Western historical-critical one; and devotional Muslim writers such as Tariq Ramadan read his life chiefly for its spiritual and ethical teaching. The editor does not rule on his prophethood, the revelation, the miracles, or his finality, and records each as the attributed belief of the tradition.
editorial_notes:
This is among the most neutrality-sensitive entries in the dataset, and it follows the register separation used in jesus-of-nazareth. (a) The historical narrative is attributed to the biographical tradition as weighed by modern historians (Watt, Donner), and its dates rest on that tradition; (b) prophethood, revelation, miracles, and his status as seal of the prophets appear only as the attributed confession of Muslims ('In Islamic belief', 'Muslims hold'), never asserted or denied in editorial voice. The phrase 'messages that he presented as revelations' in the historical paragraph is a historian's description of his proclamation, not a judgment on its source. Roles list the confessional title only with the qualifier 'in Islamic belief'.

The source-critical debate is recorded as a debate: the revisionist positions (Wansbrough; Crone and Cook) and the responses (Schoeler, Motzki, Donner) are attributed to their authors and not ranked. Crone and Cook's use of seventh-century non-Muslim sources is described as their method; per neutrality #11, no non-Muslim or polemical source is cited here as evidence for what Islam teaches or for events of the life.

Muslim practice pairs the Prophet's name with the honorific formula sallallahu alayhi wa-sallam ('may God bless him and grant him peace', often abbreviated in English as SAW or PBUH, and rendered by the sign ﷺ). The descriptive prose omits it, following academic convention, and records it here as a practice of the tradition; its omission is a register choice, not a statement of stance.

Dates: the birth year c. 570 is the traditional dating (the 'Year of the Elephant') and is approximate; hijri and CE years are given as AH/CE. Sourcing triangulates three lenses: (a) Western academic scholarship (Watt 1961; Donner 2010; Motzki 2000; Schoeler 2011; Wansbrough 1978; Crone and Cook 1977); (b) classical primary texts (the Qur'an; Ibn Ishaq in Ibn Hisham's recension, via Guillaume's translation; al-Tabari's History, vols. 6 and 9; Sahih al-Bukhari); (c) contemporary Muslim scholars (Tarif Khalidi 2009; Jonathan A. C. Brown 2011; S. H. M. Jafri 1979 for the Shi'i vantage), with Tariq Ramadan 2007 cited explicitly as a devotional Muslim voice rather than as scholarship. The succession positions are sourced to Madelung 1997 and Jafri 1979 (Sunni and Shi'i accounts) and Hoffman 2012 (Ibadi), rated as in first-fitna and rashidun. No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited. Confidence is high for the Qur'anic verses (Q 96:1-5, 33:40, 18:110, 3:144, 17:1, 9:40, read in the Saheeh International translation served by quran.com), for the Bukhari report on the first revelation (hadith 3, read verbatim in the Muhsin Khan translation via the fawazahmed0 hadith-api mirror of that edition, because sunnah.com blocked automated access; the url points to the standard sunnah.com location of the same report), and for Guillaume's translation, whose introduction (pp. xiii-xli) and Ibn Hisham's notes (p. 691) were read in the archive.org scan. All other monographs are medium: verified to exist and to treat the topic, not read line-by-line. Hagarism is presented as its authors' exploratory thesis at the time of publication, not as their settled or final view.

lifespan.note: Birth c. 570 CE on the traditional dating (the 'Year of the Elephant'), approximate. First revelation c. 610; Hijra 622 (1 AH); death in Medina in Rabi al-Awwal 11 AH, June 632 CE.

relations.note: In Islamic belief Muhammad is a prophet (nabi) and messenger (rasul); the doctrine of prophethood is the frame through which the tradition understands his mission.
The title 'seal of the prophets' (Q 33:40) is applied to Muhammad in the Qur'an, and the doctrine of the finality of his prophethood derives from it; recorded as an attributed Islamic belief.
Islamic belief holds the Qur'an to be Muhammad's principal miracle, with further miracles reported in hadith and sira; recorded as an attributed belief.
Islamic theology discusses the protection of prophets from sin and error ('isma), with Shi'i and Sunni schools holding differing extents of it, and applies the doctrine to Muhammad.
Muhammad is the founding figure of Islam; Muslims hold that he conveyed the final revelation rather than founding a new religion, understanding Islam as the religion of all the prophets.
His emigration from Mecca to Medina in 622, the event from which the hijri calendar is counted.
The document traditionally attributed to Muhammad that set out the arrangements between the emigrants, the Medinan groups, and their allies after the Hijra.
Ibn Ishaq's biography, surviving in Ibn Hisham's recension, is the earliest extant full narrative of Muhammad's life and the main source for its detailed chronology.
Muslims hold that the Qur'an revealed to Muhammad was collected into the standard codex under the caliph Uthman.
The Qur'an presents Muhammad's message as a renewal of the religion of Ibrahim (millat Ibrahim), whom Muslims hold to be an earlier prophet.
Early companion and father-in-law; in Sunni tradition his first successor as caliph, and in the Muslim account his companion in the cave during the Hijra (Q 9:40 as read by the tradition).
Companion and father-in-law; second caliph in Sunni reckoning.
Companion and son-in-law; third caliph in Sunni reckoning.

Cousin and son-in-law; Shi'i tradition holds that Muhammad designated him as successor (notably at Ghadir Khumm), while Sunni tradition counts him the fourth caliph (the positions as reconstructed by Madelung 1997 and Jafri 1979).
